title: How to choose safe investment options during rising interest rates
description: Why bonds fall when rates rise, and where to hide for safety.
content:
When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates to fight inflation, the financial landscape changes drastically. The 'Safe' investments of yesterday (Long-Term Bonds) suddenly become risky, losing value rapidly. However, rising rates are good news for savers who know where to look. They create opportunities to earn 5%+ returns with zero risk, something that wasn't possible for a decade. This guide explains how to pivot your portfolio when the Fed is hawkish.

Key Takeaways

  • Duration Risk: When rates rise, bond prices fall. Long-term bonds fall the hardest. You must shorten your duration (buy T-Bills, not T-Bonds) to protect principal.
  • Floating Rate Notes (FRN): These are special bonds where the interest payout rises automatically as benchmark rates rise. They are the ultimate hedge against rate hikes.
  • Cash is King: In a rising rate environment, cash gets a 'pay raise' every time the Fed meets. High-Yield Savings Accounts become legitimate investments.
  • Avoid High P/E Stocks: Rising rates hurt 'Growth' stocks (Tech) more than 'Value' stocks (Banks/Energy). Adjust your equity tilt.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 2022 market was a brutal lesson in 'Duration Risk.' Long-term Treasuries (TLT) lost 30%+ because rates spiked from 0% to 4%. Understanding the math of 'Duration' is mandatory for any bond investor in the US.

The Menu for Rising Rates

Where to put money when the Fed says "Rates are going Higher".

1. US Treasury Bills (Short Term)

Strategy: Buy 3-month or 6-month bills. When they mature, you reinvest at the new, higher rate. You ride the wave up.

2. Floating Rate Treasuries (USFR / TFLO)

Strategy: These ETFs hold notes that reset their interest rate daily or weekly. They have almost zero price volatility but their yield climbs instantly with the Fed Funds Rate. This is the perfect parking spot for cash.

3. Series I Savings Bonds

Strategy: Their variable rate component adjusts every 6 months based on inflation. If rates are rising due to inflation, I-Bonds pay out massively (they hit 9.62% in 2022).

What to SELL

Get out of Long-Term Corporate Bonds and 20-Year Treasuries. The longer the maturity, the more price value you lose for every 1% rate hike.

The Pivot Strategy

  1. Audit Bond Funds: Look at your bond ETF's 'Average Duration.' If it is >6 years, it is risky in a rising rate environment. Switch to a 'Short Term' bond fund (Duration < 2 years).
  2. Ladder CDs: Build a short-term ladder (3, 6, 9 months). Do not lock in a 5-year CD today if rates will be 2% higher next year.
  3. Pay Floating Debt: If you have a HELOC or variable-rate student loan, pay it off aggressively. Your interest cost is about to explode.
  4. Check Savings Banks: Banks are slow to raise rates. If the Fed hikes but your bank stays at 0.5%, switch banks immediately. Loyalty is expensive.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do stocks fall when rates rise?

Higher rates mean borrowing money is expensive for companies. It also means 'Safe' bonds pay more, making risky stocks less attractive by comparison (TINA is over).

Is it safe to buy a house?

High rates mean high mortgage payments. However, high rates usually cool off home prices. It's a trade-off. Date the rate, marry the house.

When should I buy long-term bonds again?

When the Fed signals they are done hiking and might start cutting. That is the moment to lock in the high rates for 20 years.
